operations.before: Timed positions

operations.value: Supplied teaching record: a body released from rest falls approximately 0 m, 4.90 m and 19.60 m after 0 s, 1 s and 2 s. Downward displacement is positive. Treat near-surface acceleration as constant over this short drop and neglect air resistance. These rounded values are an idealized dossier, not a transcription of Newton’s experiments.

operations.value: Fall: downward; Moon: velocity keeps turning
operations.before: Direction diagram

operations.value: Velocity includes direction as well as speed. The fall record is straight downward. In the circular approximation for the Moon, speed stays constant but the velocity turns; acceleration points inward toward Earth. Acceleration is change of velocity per unit time, not distance fallen.
operations.before: Modern arrows distinguish a changing direction from a mere increase in speed.

operations.value: Surface fall: ≈4.90 m in 1 s from rest
operations.before: Falling-body record

operations.value: The supplied near-surface record gives approximately 4.90 m of downward displacement in 1 s after release from rest. Ignore air resistance and use constant local acceleration. operations.before: An idealized low-resistance record; the model’s conditions are stated, not assumed to hold in every medium.

operations.value: 1 kg and 2 kg: same idealized fall
operations.before: Mass comparison

operations.before: Two supplied test cases distinguish mass from velocity and force.

operations.value: Moon: ≈60 Earth radii; ≈27.3-day circuit
operations.before: Orbit distances

operations.value: Independent supplied orbital inputs, not values fitted from the 4.90 m fall: Earth radius R ≈ 6.37 million m; lunar distance r ≈ 60R ≈ 382.2 million m; orbital period T ≈ 27.3 days ≈ 2,358,720 s. Under a circular, fixed-Earth, short-time approximation, the geometric construction gives an inward departure from the initial tangent of about 1.36 mm in 1 s. Ignore eccentricity, solar perturbations and Earth’s motion about the Earth–Moon barycentre. These are rounded teaching inputs, not Newton’s exact historical numbers.
operations.before: Distances and periods permit a check across more than one planetary path.

operations.value: Candidate: inward acceleration ∝ 1/r²
operations.before: Candidate force rule

operations.value: Proposed Earth-centred rule: a(r) = a(R) × (R/r)², with r measured from Earth’s centre and R its radius. This is a rule for acceleration; force on a test body is F = ma. For the same short time Δt, displacement from an initially tangent straight path is approximately d = ½a(Δt)². A body released from rest falls the same distance under the same constant acceleration. The rule is a candidate to compare with independently supplied orbit data.
operations.before: A central inverse-square relation is proposed for the mathematical exercise; fitting is not an origin story.

operations.value: Successive 1 s averages: 4.90 → 14.70 m/s
operations.before: Motion differences

These are average downward velocities over successive intervals, not the endpoint speeds. Under the stated constant-acceleration assumption, they equal the velocities at the interval midpoints, 0.5 s and 1.5 s.
operations.before: Displacement over equal times separates steady motion from changing motion.

operations.before: Acceleration record

operations.before: Force comparison

operations.value: Circle + tangent: d≈2π²r(Δt/T)²
operations.before: Orbital geometry

operations.value: Carry forward two mathematical habits: state the geometric premises, and compare a calculated position with a recorded one. For a circular orbit of radius r and period T, an elapsed time Δt turns through θ = 2πΔt/T. The inward distance from the initial tangent is r(1−cos θ), approximately rθ²/2 for this very short interval; hence d ≈ 2π²r(Δt/T)². This supplied modern construction extends the earlier geometry; Euclid’s triangle proof alone did not establish orbital dynamics. The tangent is straight continuation at the initial velocity, not the distance remaining to Earth.
operations.before: The recorded orbit constrains a geometric account rather than being replaced by a decorative circle.

operations.value: Same short time: d(r)/d(R)≈(R/r)²
operations.before: Orbit model

operations.value: Join the circular construction to the candidate acceleration rule. Since d ≈ ½a(Δt)², equal short time intervals cancel from the ratio: d(r)/d(R) ≈ a(r)/a(R) = (R/r)². Thus orbital departure and a fall from rest can be compared without confusing displacement with acceleration. The orbital construction supplies a separate value to check; the distance law does not manufacture that observation.
operations.before: The proposed force is used to calculate orbital behavior, making consequences available for comparison.

operations.value: Moon: ≈1.36 mm in 1 s; rule gives 1/3600
operations.before: Cross-orbit check

operations.value: Insert the supplied lunar radius and period into the circular construction: 2π² × 382,200,000 m × (1 s / 2,358,720 s)² ≈ 0.001356 m, or 1.36 mm of inward departure in 1 s. Separately, r ≈ 60R makes the candidate ratio 1/60² = 1/3600. The terrestrial branch must now supply the surface fall for comparison. This is one Moon-distance check, not a claim to have tested several planetary orbits.
operations.before: More than one orbit tests the relation; reproducing a single chosen path would be weaker evidence.

operations.value: 4.90 m ÷ 60² ≈ 1.36 mm: matches Moon
operations.before: Shared motion account

operations.value: Scale the terrestrial displacement by the candidate inverse-square ratio: 4.90 m ÷ 60² = 0.001361… m ≈ 1.36 mm in 1 s. The separate orbit calculation gave 0.001356… m ≈ 1.36 mm in 1 s: agreement at the stated rounding, not exact equality. Equivalently, 9.80 m/s² ÷ 3600 ≈ 0.00272 m/s². Keeping surface acceleration unchanged at the lunar distance would instead predict 4.90 m in 1 s, about 3600 times too much. This comparison supports one quantitative account of the two motions under the stated idealizations.
operations.before: One mathematical framework addresses terrestrial and celestial cases without making every physical mechanism known.

operations.value: Earth and Moon fit; gravity’s cause stays open
operations.before: Scope of law

operations.value: The fall and lunar departure agree with the proposed inverse-square scaling at this precision. That is an achievement, not a demonstration of gravity’s ultimate physical cause. One rounded comparison also does not uniquely fix every possible distance law or test every orbit. Newton’s later General Scholium separates the successful gravitational account from an established cause. No numerical vortex theory has been tested in this exercise, and mathematical agreement does not compel a particular theology.
operations.before: Predictive success is distinguished from an ultimate explanation of gravity. Mathematical laws do not compel a particular theology.

operations.value: Earth → Moon: 4.90 m ÷ 3600 ≈ 1.36 mm
operations.before: Mathematical treatise

operations.value: The checked account preserves a calculable claim: over the same 1 s, a 4.90 m surface fall divided by 60² agrees, at the supplied precision, with the Moon’s separately orbit-derived 1.36 mm inward departure. Algebra kept operations and units consistent; geometry turned radius and period into departure from a tangent; the earlier sky caution limits the inference. The circular, short-time, fixed-Earth and negligible-resistance idealizations remain attached. This supports shared gravitational scaling, not a measured exact equality, a proof of every orbit, or gravity’s ultimate cause.
operations.before: The account can be inspected, calculated from and criticized; publication does not make its conditions disappear.

operations.value: A surface body falls about 4.90 m in 1 s; the Moon departs from its tangent by about 1.36 mm in the same time. Can the proposed inverse-square rule connect them at a distance of about 60 Earth radii? Keep the calculation distinct from gravity’s ultimate cause.
operations.before: A planetary orbit and a falling body appear to be different problems. Make a mathematical account that answers both without claiming to know gravity’s ultimate cause.
